subtype: Turning away as boundary or snub [Interpreting]
passage: At the lockers of their Toronto high school, Camila spotted Bao and called, "Bao! Did you see the new art room?" Bao glanced at her, then turned his whole body towards the wall and pressed his forehead against his locker door. Camila's wave froze in the air. Great. What did I do? All through Spanish she replayed Friday: had she laughed too loudly at his drawing? She almost left him out of the plan for Saturday. Instead, after school, she found him on the bus bench and sat down a little distance away. "Hey. Earlier, did I do something?" Bao rubbed his eyes. "No. My grandma's in hospital. I'd just got a text. I couldn't talk to anyone." Camila nodded and simply sat with him until his bus came.

qa.q: What did Camila call out to Bao about?
qa.a: The new art room.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling when her wave froze in the air?
qa.a: Camila felt hurt and worried, sure she had done something wrong and replaying Friday to find it.

qa.q: What kept Camila's friendship with Bao steady?
qa.a: Not acting on the snub, such as leaving him out of Saturday's plan, and asking him quietly later instead.

qa.q: What was that moment at the lockers like for Bao?
qa.a: Bao had just learned his grandma was in hospital and was too upset to talk to anyone; turning away had nothing to do with Camila.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reading a friend turning away as a snub when the friend needed space, and asking later instead of taking it personally.

passage:
Coach's notes, inter-school badminton final
During warm-up I noticed Abhinav's shoulders were almost touching his ears. He was gripping the racket hard, and his smashes kept going into the net. Kashish, his doubles partner, spotted it before I did. She walked over and said, "Do the thing," and they both rolled their shoulders back slowly, five times, breathing out on each roll. Abhinav's shoulders dropped visibly; I could see it from the bench. His next smash was clean. At the change of ends in the second game, when they were behind, I saw him check himself, roll once without anyone reminding him, and reset. They lost narrowly, but he played loose and brave. Next step: I am making the shoulder roll part of every team's warm-up and asking Kashish to demonstrate it.

qa.q: Who is Abhinav's doubles partner?
qa.a: Kashish.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling during warm-up, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was anxious and tense before the final: shoulders near his ears, a hard grip, and smashes going into the net.

qa.q: What shows the shoulder roll had become Abhinav's own tool?
qa.a: In the second game, when they were behind, he rolled once without being reminded and reset.

qa.q: How did Kashish read Abhinav's shoulders?
qa.a: Kashish recognised the raised shoulders as nerves and offered their calming routine without making a fuss.

grounding: It shows a teenager holding tension in raised shoulders before a match and learning to notice and release it with a slow shoulder roll.

passage: In their small house behind the Satara bus depot, Yash looked up from mending the bicycle tyre. "So, the district quiz. How did it go?" Omkar shrugged and dropped his bag. "Fine." He went to the water pot. Yash wanted to say, "Just fine? After two months of practice?" He didn't. He kept patching the tube and asked, "Tell me about the hardest question." Omkar drank slowly. "There was one on rivers. I knew it. I actually knew it, and I froze, and Sachin answered." He shrugged again, but this time his voice cracked. "We came fourth." Yash put down the tube. "You froze on one you knew. That's the part that hurts, isn't it?" Omkar nodded, sat down on the step beside him, and finally told the whole story.

qa.q: What was Yash mending?
qa.a: The bicycle tyre.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling behind the second shrug?
qa.a: Omkar was upset and ashamed about freezing on a question he knew, even though the first shrug looked as if he didn't care.

qa.q: Which question unlocked Omkar's real answer, and why?
qa.a: Asking about the hardest question, which invited a story instead of a one-word reply, while Yash kept calmly working.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt when Omkar just said "Fine"?
qa.a: Yash was probably disappointed and curious after two months of practice, but he held back his frustration.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager's shrug at a parent's question hiding upset, and a patient open question unlocking the real answer.

subtype: Folded arms as boundary or comfort [Mismatch]
passage:
Dear Deepika Ma'am,
I'm writing because of what you said after debate practice today, that I look "closed-off" when I fold my arms and that judges might mark me down. I've been thinking about it all evening. Honestly, there are three reasons I fold them. The auditorium AC is freezing and I always forget my sweater. Also, when I'm waiting to speak, holding my arms feels like holding myself together; it calms me. And only sometimes, like when Rohan interrupted me three times, it's me saying "stop". I didn't want you to think I was being rude to the team. I will try keeping my hands on the lectern when I speak. Could you tell me if I start looking closed-off again, so I can check which reason it is?
Thank you,
Wasim

qa.q: Who interrupted Wasim three times?
qa.a: Rohan.

qa.q: How was Wasim feeling while writing the email?
qa.a: Wasim felt worried and a little misunderstood, anxious that Deepika Ma'am thought the folded arms meant rudeness to the team.

qa.q: What plan did Wasim suggest, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Keeping hands on the lectern while speaking and asking Ma'am to point out the folded arms, so they can check which reason it is rather than guess.

qa.q: How might Deepika Ma'am read the email?
qa.a: Deepika Ma'am may be surprised that the folded arms usually meant cold or self-calming, and glad Wasim explained instead of sulking.

grounding: It shows a teenager's folded arms meaning cold, comfort or a boundary, and why reading them as closed-off without checking can be unfair.

passage: Rain was hammering the tin shelter outside the coaching centre, and the bus was due in five minutes. Dilnaz came out with her mock result crumpled in her fist, eyes red. Vikas started to open his arms, then stopped halfway. With everyone crowded under the shelter and the rain so loud, he had to lean close to be heard. "Do you want a hug, or no?" Dilnaz shook her head and folded her arms tight. "Not here. Not now." "Okay." Vikas lowered his arms and tilted his umbrella so it covered her instead. "Want me to just stand here?" She nodded. They stood side by side, not touching, until the bus splashed up. On the bus she finally said, "Thanks for asking first." He shrugged. "It's your call, always."

qa.q: What was Dilnaz holding in her fist?
qa.a: Her crumpled mock result.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he stopped with his arms halfway open?
qa.a: He felt caring and wanted to comfort Dilnaz, but was unsure whether a hug would be welcome in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did Vikas still comfort Dilnaz after she said no?
qa.a: He lowered his arms without fuss, tilted the umbrella over her, and offered simply to stand with her.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Vikas asked first?
qa.a: Dilnaz likely felt respected and less exposed, free to say no and still be supported 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a teenager opening his arms to comfort an upset friend, asking first whether a hug is welcome, and respecting her refusal.

subtype: Clapping and snapping in peer groups [Expressing]
passage:
"Okay, that verse was brilliant," Neelam said, snapping her fingers fast, snap-snap-snap. "Again!"
Raghav grinned and rapped the chorus again, and the others joined the snapping.
"Now the second verse," said Tenzin.
Raghav started, stumbled on "catastrophe", and stopped.
Clap. Clap. Clap. Neelam brought her hands together slowly, eyebrows high. The group laughed.
Raghav didn't. "Wow. Thanks."
Neelam's hands stopped. "Wait, I was joking."
"A slow clap isn't a joke when I've just messed up in front of everyone."
Neelam dropped her hands. "You're right. That was laughing at you, not with you. Sorry." She turned to the others. "He wrote that whole verse himself, you know." Then she snapped, fast and loud. "From the top. You've got it."
Raghav took a breath and nailed it.

qa.q: Which word did Raghav stumble on?
qa.a: "Catastrophe".

qa.q: Why did Neelam's hands stop?
qa.a: Neelam felt surprised and then guilty on seeing that the joking slow clap had stung Raghav.

qa.q: How did Neelam repair things?
qa.a: She admitted it was laughing at him, apologised, praised his verse to the group and switched back to fast, supportive snapping.

qa.q: What was the slow clap like for Raghav?
qa.a: Coming right after he stumbled, it felt like mockery in front of the group, and it hurt.

grounding: It shows fast snapping as approval and a slow clap as mockery among friends, with speed and tone deciding which it is.

passage:
"I swear, Aman, I didn't tell anyone about your audition." Parveen held both palms open towards him. "Look. Nothing to hide."
Amandeep studied her hands. "Mehul says you told him."
"Mehul says a lot of things."
"You're doing the open-palms thing. Like those videos say honest people do."
"Because I am honest!"
"Maybe. But anyone can open their hands." Amandeep sighed. "I don't want to decide from your hands. Did you tell anyone at all? Even by accident?"
Parveen lowered her hands slowly. "I told my sister. At home. Mehul was on a video call with her."
"So not on purpose."
"No. But it got out because of me. I'm sorry."
Amandeep nodded. "Thanks for telling me what really happened."

qa.q: What had Amandeep kept secret?
qa.a: An audition.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling while studying Parveen's hands?
qa.a: He felt hurt and suspicious after hearing from Mehul, but also unsure, and didn't want to judge from her hands alone.

qa.q: Why was Amandeep's question better than trusting the open palms?
qa.a: Open palms are one cue, not proof either way; a specific question brought out what had actually happened.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when asked "Even by accident?"
qa.a: Parveen probably felt guilty, and relieved to be given a way to tell the whole truth, since the leak wasn't on purpose.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager treating open palms as one cue, not proof of honesty, and asking a clear question instead.

passage: The inter-school football match in Darjeeling went ahead in a thin, cold drizzle, with their usual coach away at a wedding. Every time Dolma touched the ball, Pema from the other team jogged past and gave her a thumbs-down right in her face. By the second half it had become the raised middle finger, twice, and a muttered word Dolma wouldn't repeat. Her own hand twitched to give it straight back. She didn't. She stepped away, took a breath of the wet air, and jogged to the touchline, where Mr Lepcha, the substitute teacher, stood with an umbrella. "Sir, number 9 keeps making rude signs at me. It's been all match." Mr Lepcha thanked her, spoke to the referee at once, and Pema was cautioned. After the match he told the other school's teacher, and that evening he rang Dolma's mother.

qa.q: Why was the usual coach away?
qa.a: The coach was at a wedding.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when her hand twitched?
qa.a: She felt angry and insulted, tempted to give the gesture straight back, but chose to stay calm.

qa.q: Which steps did Dolma take, and how did Mr Lepcha respond?
qa.a: She stepped away, breathed and told Mr Lepcha, who spoke to the referee at once, told the other school's teacher and rang her mother that evening.

qa.q: What would change if Dolma had given the gesture back?
qa.a: Dolma could have been cautioned too, and the adults might have seen a two-way fight instead of one player being targeted.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager recognising repeated thumbs-down and rude gestures as targeted insults, staying calm, and telling an adult who acts the same day.

passage:
Monday: The first online class of flood week. Kiran unmuted to answer and talked straight over Ayesha, who had started at the same moment. Both stopped. Both started again. Ms Rao laughed. "Let's use the raise-hand button."
Wednesday: Kiran clicked the little hand and waited; when Ms Rao called on him, he unmuted, answered, and muted again. Ayesha's square stayed dark all class, and she didn't answer when called. Kiran wondered if she was bored, or still upset about Monday. After class he messaged her: "all ok? you went quiet." She replied: "power cut + my net keeps freezing. could hear only half."
Friday: Ayesha's connection held. She raised her hand, Kiran sent a 👍 in the chat when she finished, and nobody talked over anyone.

qa.q: Why was Ayesha quiet on Wednesday?
qa.a: There was a power cut and her net kept freezing, so she could hear only half.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling about Ayesha's dark square?
qa.a: Kiran felt unsure and a little worried, wondering whether she was bored or still upset about Monday.

qa.q: What helped Kiran read Ayesha's silence fairly?
qa.a: He didn't assume; he messaged her privately to check, which showed the real reason was a power cut and lag.

qa.q: What was Wednesday's class like for Ayesha?
qa.a: Ayesha was probably frustrated, hearing only half the lesson on a freezing connection and unable to answer.

grounding: It shows a teenager using the raise-hand and mute tools to take turns online, and learning that silence in a video call can mean lag rather than disengagement.
